> "I did not have outside help. I didn't even use the book after reading. Just this discussion. I understand the force between charged objects, but what IS charge? I see why atoms are charged, but the book didn't explain why electrons or protons, or even neutrons have the charge that they do."

|---------|------------|----------|

| Direction of the force & Newton's third law | Understood | Correctly identified that the forces on each charge are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction ("they will always point in opposite directions"), connecting this to Newton's third law. |
| Properties of charge — quantization, conservation, magnitude symmetry | Understood | Correctly identified quantization ("charges are discrete... integer numbers of charges"), conservation ("I don't think they can be destroyed"), and that the magnitudes of positive and negative elementary charge are equal. |
| Conductors, insulators & charging by induction | Partial | Gave a good intuitive explanation of polarization and why neutral objects are attracted to charged ones, but did not explicitly distinguish conductors from insulators in terms of free conduction electrons, and charging by induction was not reached. |

The cadet understands how atoms become charged and how the force behaves, but wants to know why electrons, protons, and neutrons have the intrinsic charges they do. This is a genuine and sophisticated question — it goes beyond the scope of the reading and into particle physics.

## Lateral Connections Raised

🟡 **Yellow — Soft on specific topics.**

**Specifics for Yellow:** The cadet has a solid grasp of Coulomb's law, charge properties, and polarization, but the conductor/insulator distinction (free conduction electrons vs. bound electrons) and charging by induction were not fully covered. The cadet understands *that* polarization causes attraction of neutral objects to charged ones, but did not explicitly articulate *why conductors behave differently from insulators* in holding static charge. Worth a brief touch in class.

## Tutor's Honest Notes

Ellis came in well-prepared and engaged thoughtfully throughout. The cadet's core question — what charge *fundamentally is* — is a genuinely deep one that the reading does not answer, and reflects real intellectual curiosity rather than a gap in the assigned material. The conversation ran long due to the natural flow of discussion, which left charging by induction uncovered; the instructor may want to give that topic brief attention. No misconceptions were observed and the cadet's reasoning was generally sound and self-correcting.
